Chapter 7: Redefining Success and Failure
When you think about success, what comes to mind? For a lot of us, it’s all about recognition, money, or maybe getting a thumbs-up from others. And failure? That’s something most people try to dodge—a sign that maybe the work wasn’t good enough, or worse, that *we* weren’t good enough. But living creatively? It asks us to see things differently. It’s not about the result—it’s about the *making* itself. Picture this: someone pours months of their heart into a painting, only to have it turned down by a local gallery. That sting of rejection? It’s real. And it’s tempting to just give up, right there. But once the initial disappointment fades, something else comes into focus. The real value wasn’t in the gallery’s approval—it was in the hours spent painting, in the way the work shaped the artist, and in the courage it took to even try. That rejection? It’s not the whole story. It’s just one stop along the way.
Here’s another example—a songwriter sends out demo after demo to record labels, and all they get is silence. Every unanswered submission feels like a tiny defeat. Still, the songwriter keeps at it, writing new songs and sending them out again. And then, finally, one song lands with a small audience. From there, new doors start to open. Looking back, it turns out those so-called failures weren’t wasted at all. Each one taught something vital—about bouncing back, about honing the craft, about trusting yourself to keep going.
You know, most people don’t realize that success and failure aren’t enemies—they’re actually partners in this whole creative process. Every single attempt, whether it’s met with applause or just quiet, is an opportunity: a moment to learn, to grow, to discover something you didn’t know before. And it’s the willingness to risk failure that actually opens the door to real success.
It’s easy to slip into the habit of measuring your work by what others think, or by external rewards. But here’s something to pay attention to—the most meaningful victories are often the ones you can’t see. The deep satisfaction of finishing a project, the pride in pushing through a tough challenge, the joy you get from sharing something that’s honest and real—these are the true markers of creative success.
So, if you take one thing away from this: failure isn’t the end of the road. It’s actually a sign that you tried, that you took a chance, that you cared enough to put yourself out there. And honestly? That’s where the magic of growth really happens.
